# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="push") — the large button
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I am the Blind monkey. I can feel the bomb but cannot see colors or read the manual. My view confirms there is a large button and three wires, but all visual details (colors, labels) are unknown to me.

I need information from Deaf (who sees colors/labels) and Mute (who reads the manual).
Deaf can see my gestures. Mute can hear my speech.
I will speak to Mute to ask for the manual's rules regarding this specific configuration.
I will gesture to Deaf to ask for the visual state of the wires and display.

For Deaf: I need to know the colors of the wires (1, 2, 3) and what is on the display.
Since I don't have a pre-agreed code, I will use simple gestures to indicate "Wire 1", "Wire 2", "Wire 3" and "Display".
However, without a shared language, this is risky.
Let's try to establish a basic query.
To Deaf: Pointing at wire positions? No, they can't see me point at the bomb if I'm blind? Wait, Deaf *sees* the bomb. Deaf sees *me*.
If I gesture "1", "2", "3" using fingers, Deaf might interpret that as asking about those wires.
But how do I ask for colors?
Maybe I should just wait for them to volunteer info? The prompt says "Work together." Usually, in these puzzles, you have to ask.

Let's assume standard finger counting for indices.
Gesture to Deaf: ✌️ (2), ☝️ (1), 👆 (pointing up? or 1?), 🖐️ (5?).
This is too ambiguous.

Alternative strategy:
The "Speech" section says: "A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced... whoever holds one can describe it, never read it out."
Colors are marks. Deaf sees them. Deaf cannot speak. Deaf must gesture them? But gestures are limited symbols.
Unless we agree on a mapping.

Let's look at the channels again.
Blind -> Speak -> Mute.
Blind -> Gesture -> Deaf & Mute.

Mute knows the manual. Mute needs to know what the bomb looks like to tell us what to do.
Deaf knows what it looks like. Deaf needs to tell Mute.
Deaf can gesture to Mute. Mute can see gestures.
So Deaf -> Gesture -> Mute.
Mute -> Speak -> Blind.
Blind -> Act.

This seems like the most logical chain.
1. Deaf describes the bomb to Mute via gestures.
2. Mute interprets the manual and tells Blind what to do via speech.
3. Blind acts.

In Turn 1, I (Blind) don't know anything yet. I should probably stay silent or signal readiness?
If I speak now, I might confuse Mute who doesn't know the state yet.
If I gesture now, Deaf might not understand what I want.

However, often the first turn requires establishing contact.
Let's try to prompt Deaf to start describing.
I can gesture "Please" or "Look"?
🙏 (Prayer hands) might mean "Please help" or "Wait".
👋 (Wave) might mean "Hello" or "Start".

Let's gesture to Deaf: 👋 (to get attention/start) then maybe pointing?
Actually, if Deaf sees the bomb, they should start describing it to Mute immediately if they realize Mute needs it.
But do they know Mute needs it? Yes, Mute is the only one who can read the manual.

Let's assume the other monkeys are intelligent agents following the same logic.
Deaf sees the bomb. Deaf knows Mute can read the manual. Deaf knows Blind is the hands.
Deaf should gesture to Mute.

If I send nothing, does time pass? "wait()".
If everyone waits, nothing happens.

I should probably signal that I am ready to act, or ask for instructions.
Speaking to Mute: "Ready."
Gesturing to Deaf: "Go."

Let's try to initiate the flow.
I will speak to Mute: "What do I do?"
I will gesture to Deaf: "Describe to Mute." (Hard to encode).

Let's stick to the simplest interpretation:
I am Blind. I see nothing. I feel the parts.
I will ask Mute for instructions.
`speak(to="mute", text="instructions")`

And I will signal Deaf to communicate with Mute.
`gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👉", "🤟"])`? No, arbitrary.

Let's try `wait()`? No, that stalls.

Let's assume a common protocol isn't established.
I will speak to Mute asking for the plan.
I will gesture to Deaf asking for visual data?
Actually, Deaf cannot speak. Deaf MUST gesture to Mute.
Does Deaf know to gesture to Mute?
If Deaf gestures to Mute, Mute hears nothing (Mute is mute, but can Mute hear? "Mute ... Cannot ... Speak". It doesn't say Mute cannot hear. "Whoever can hear receives your words". Mute can likely hear.)
Yes, Mute can hear Blind's speech. Mute can see Deaf's gestures.

So:
1. Deaf gestures to Mute (describing bomb).
2. Mute speaks to Blind (giving orders).
3. Blind acts.

In Turn 1, I (Blind) should probably just listen/wait for Mute?
But Mute won't speak until Mute gets info from Deaf.
Will Deaf gesture to Mute unprompted?
If Deaf is also waiting for a prompt...

I will gesture to Deaf: "Talk to Mute".
How?
Point at Mute? I don't know where Mute is.
Point at myself?
Maybe just "Help".

Let's try a different angle.
The prompt implies I should take action.
I will speak to Mute: "Waiting for instructions."
I will gesture to Deaf: "Show Mute."

Symbols:
👉 (Right)
🤟 (Love/ILY?)
✋ (Stop/Hand)

Let's try to be less specific and more open.
I'll just speak to Mute. If Mute is smart, they'll ask Deaf. But Mute can't speak.
So Mute is stuck unless Deaf acts.

I will gesture to Deaf: **👀** (Eyes)? Not in alphabet.
**✋** (Hand) **👉** (Point) **🤟**?

Let's look at the alphabet again.
👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

I will gesture to Deaf: **👋** (Hello/Attention) followed by **🤝** (Cooperation/Link).
Meaning: "Hey, let's work together."

And speak to Mute: "Need input."

```
speak(to="mute", text="need input")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🤝"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: The light is green. The button is large and says PUSH TO DEFUSE. There are three wires: 1 is red, 2 is green, 3 is yellow.

I am the Blind monkey. I have just received information from Deaf (who can see) about the visual state of the bomb:
- Light: Green
- Button: Large, smooth, says "PUSH TO DEFUSE"
- Wires: 1 is Red, 2 is Green, 3 is Yellow

I cannot see these things, but I know them now because Deaf told me.
Mute has not spoken yet. Mute holds the manual.
The standard logic for this puzzle type is:
1. Deaf describes visuals to the group (or specifically to those who need it). Here, Deaf spoke to *me* (Blind). Wait, the prompt says "Deaf says to Blind". This implies Deaf used speech? But Deaf is "Deaf". The table says Deaf **Cannot** hear anything. It doesn't explicitly say Deaf cannot speak, but usually "Deaf" in these riddles implies they cannot hear, and often are mute or use sign language. However, the context says "Deaf says to Blind...". If Deaf *spoke*, I would hear it. But I am Blind. Can I hear? Yes, only sight is missing. So Deaf spoke to me.
   - Rule check: "Whoever can hear receives your words". Deaf cannot hear. Does Deaf speak? The role description for Deaf says "Can See... Cannot Hear... or touch". It does not list "Cannot Speak". So Deaf can speak.
   - Okay, so Deaf gave me the visual data directly via voice.

Now I have the visual data. I still need the *rules* from Mute.
Mute has not spoken yet. Mute might be waiting for us to establish that we have the visual data, or Mute might be confused about what to do without knowing if we understand the situation.
Or, perhaps Mute needs to know what I feel? No, I've described my reach (push/cut).
Maybe Mute needs to know the configuration to consult the manual.
Since Deaf already told me the colors, I should relay this to Mute so Mute can look up the correct procedure in the manual.

My turn:
1. Inform Mute of the current state (Light Green, Wire Colors R/G/Y).
2. Ask Mute for instructions based on the manual.

I will speak to Mute. I will also gesture to Deaf to acknowledge receipt (optional, but good practice).

To Mute: "Light green. Wires: 1 red, 2 green, 3 yellow. Manual?"

```
speak(to="mute", text="light green wires 1 red 2 green 3 yellow manual")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👌"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
BUTTON [large] [smooth]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Mute points to Wire 1. Act on the first wire.

I have received a command from Deaf, who is reporting Mute's gesture.
Mute (the manual reader) has indicated that I should act on Wire 1.
Deaf says "Act on the first wire."
My available actions are `push` or `cut`. The instruction specifies the target (Wire 1) but not the specific operation verb explicitly in the text "Act on", though usually "act on a wire" implies cutting it in these bomb contexts unless specified otherwise. However, looking at my action list: `act(op="cut", position=N)` and `act(op="push")`.
The prompt says "Mute points to Wire 1". Pointing at a wire usually signifies interaction with that wire. The most common interaction with wires is cutting. Pushing is for the button.
Therefore, I will cut Wire 1.

```
act(op="cut", position=1)
```
